title: Mrunal Thakur Issues Legal Warning Over AI Deepfakes, Joins Growing List of Bollywood Stars Fighting Back
excerpt: The Bollywood actress called deepfake content using her likeness 'illegal and unacceptable' in a pointed Instagram statement, as Indian courts and regulators tighten the noose on AI-generated identity theft.
body:
• Mrunal Thakur warned deepfake creators to 'stop immediately' in a statement posted to her Instagram Story on August 4, threatening legal action against any further misuse of her identity.
  • She joins Varun Dhawan, Preity Zinta, Shashi Tharoor, and other Indian public figures who have pursued legal remedies against AI-generated content exploiting their likenesses.
  • India amended its IT Rules in February 2026, slashing the compliance window for removing deepfake content from 36 hours to three hours.
  • Courts have ordered takedowns and granted personality rights protection in a string of cases since 2023, but a comprehensive legal framework for personality rights remains absent.

Bollywood actress Mrunal Thakur has issued a sharp public warning against the creation and circulation of AI-generated deepfake content using her identity, threatening legal consequences for anyone who continues to misuse her likeness.

In a statement posted to her Instagram Story on Monday, Thakur left no room for ambiguity.

"Creating or sharing deepfake content using my likeness is illegal and unacceptable. Consider this your formal notice to stop immediately. Any further misuse of my identity will result in legal action."

— Mrunal Thakur, via Instagram Story

The statement comes amid escalating concerns over AI-driven identity theft targeting Indian celebrities, many of whom have turned to the courts for relief.

A Growing Wave of Legal Action

Thakur is the latest in a rapidly expanding list of Indian public figures pushing back against deepfake abuse. In May 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered the takedown of AI-generated deepfake content and unauthorised merchandise featuring Varun Dhawan, restraining platforms from exploiting his name, image, voice, or likeness without consent. The court directed removal of 168 identified URLs within 36 hours.

https://x.com/glamsham/status/2084600882675720375

In July 2026, the Bombay High Court intervened on behalf of actress Preity Zinta, directing social media platforms to remove approximately 275 links containing AI-generated images and morphed content that the court said infringed her privacy and personality rights. Justice Jamdar described the content as an assault on Zinta's "meticulously curated public image."

The Delhi High Court also protected Congress MP Shashi Tharoor's personality rights after AI-generated videos falsely depicted him making politically sensitive statements praising Pakistan during the 2026 Kerala election campaign. The court restrained defendants from reproducing his "visual likeness, distinct voice, signature oratorical cadence" through AI technologies.

Other Bollywood figures including Salman Khan, Shilpa Shetty, Suniel Shetty, Anil Kapoor, and Arijit Singh have secured similar protections through the courts.

India's Evolving Legal Response

India has been steadily tightening its regulatory framework around deepfakes, though experts say the approach remains reactive. In February 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021, cutting the compliance window for removing specified unlawful content — including synthetically generated or AI-manipulated audiovisual material — from 36 hours to just three hours.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=kVzQt10YZ4U

Under the amended rules, platforms must disable access to such content within three hours of receiving a lawful written order. Orders from police authorities must come from an officer not below the rank of Deputy Inspector General.

Legal experts note that enforcement remains challenging. "AI-generated impersonation can trigger overlapping civil and criminal consequences, including identity theft, cheating by personation, defamation, privacy violations and, in certain cases, offences relating to obscene or sexually explicit material," said Ankit Sahni, partner at Ajay Sahni & Associates.

A Legal Gap That Persists

Unlike the United States, where personality rights are defined as the "right of publicity" and can vary by state, or the European Union, which protects personal and biometric data under the GDPR and classifies deepfakes as high-risk under the EU AI Act 2024, India lacks an explicit statutory definition of personality rights.

Courts have stepped into this vacuum. The Delhi High Court's landmark 2023 ruling in Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India established that a "celebrity's right of endorsement acts as a major source of livelihood" that cannot be destroyed through unauthorised use. Subsequent rulings involving Aishwarya Rai Bachchan (2025) and Varun Dhawan (2026) have reinforced this principle.

But legal practitioners argue that the absence of a dedicated personality rights statute leaves enforcement fragmented and largely dependent on individual lawsuits.

Looking Ahead

Thakur's public stance reflects a shift from private legal remedies to preemptive public warnings — a strategy that carries its own weight in the age of social media, where a viral Instagram Story can reach millions before any court order is served. Whether India moves toward a comprehensive personality rights framework or continues to build its protections case by case, the pressure from its entertainment industry shows no signs of easing.
